strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and timely problem in visual brain decoding: current evaluation metrics (such as 2-way identification) are saturated and poorly aligned with human semantic perception, masking the actual errors made by generative models.

The proposed SEED metric intelligently combines complementary perspectives—object-level matching (Object F1), semantic narrative (Cap-Sim), and global deep representations (EffNet)—to achieve a state-of-the-art correlation with human judgments (0.621 Kendall's Tau-b compared to 0.368 for CLIP).

The authors collected and plan to open-source a high-quality human evaluation dataset consisting of 22 human ratings on 1,000 ground-truth/reconstruction pairs, which is a highly valuable asset for the research community.

The proposed pairwise hinge loss ($L_{pair}$) is highly practical, showing consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements when integrated into multiple state-of-the-art brain decoding models (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain).
The paper is very well-written, presenting comprehensive analyses of 'worst-case' alignments and characterizing the 'semantic near-miss phenomenon' in visual brain decoding.
weaknesses: SEED is computationally heavy, requiring the execution of several large neural networks (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, and EffNet) to evaluate a single pair of images.

Because SEED relies on generative captioning and open-vocabulary detection models, any inherent domain-specific biases, inaccuracies, or hallucinations of these auxiliary models will inevitably propagate into the evaluation score.

The mathematical formulation of the pairwise hinge loss ($L_{pair}$) is relatively standard and represents a common ranking-based objective in deep metric learning, although its application here is well-justified and effective.
The evaluation is restricted to the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD). Demonstrating generalizability on another dataset (e.g., BOLD5000) would have further strengthened the metric's robustness.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and timely problem in visual brain decoding: the inadequacy of current evaluation metrics (such as two-way identification) which are hitting ceiling effects and fail to align well with human semantic perception.

The proposed SEED metric is well-motivated and cleverly designed, combining object detection (Object F1), natural language description similarity (Cap-Sim), and robust feature correlation (EffNet) to capture complementary aspects of semantic alignment.

The authors collected and plan to open-source a valuable human judgment dataset containing 22 ratings per pair for 1,000 reconstructed images, which will benefit future evaluation and development in the visual brain decoding community.

The introduction of the Pairwise Hinge Loss is a practical and effective addition, showing consistent visual and quantitative improvements in reconstruction quality when integrated into multiple state-of-the-art brain decoding models.
The paper is exceptionally well-written and structured, with thorough analyses of worst-case failures of individual metrics, demonstrating why their combination in SEED is robust and complementary.
weaknesses: The Object F1 component is restricted to 82 categories (80 COCO categories + 2 human categories). If the decoded image contains objects outside this set, Object F1 may not capture their presence or absence, leaving the semantic evaluation to rely solely on Cap-Sim and EffNet.

The human judgment dataset only contains reconstructions from a single model (MindEye2). It would strengthen the paper's claims of generalizability if human ratings were also evaluated on reconstructions from other architectures with potentially different failure modes (e.g., UniBrain or MindBridge).

The computational cost of SEED is relatively high compared to traditional metrics, as it requires running several heavy deep learning models (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, EffNet) for evaluation. A brief discussion on the runtime/resource overhead of SEED would be beneficial.

The proposed Pairwise Hinge Loss introduces sensitive hyperparameters ($T_{pair}$ and $\lambda_{pair}$) that require model-specific tuning, as shown by the varying search spaces in the supplementary material.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and critical bottleneck in visual brain decoding: the saturation and unreliability of current evaluation metrics (e.g., 2-way identification and SSIM) in reflecting true human semantic judgments.

The authors collected a valuable dataset of 1,000 ground-truth/reconstructed image pairs evaluated by 22 human raters. Releasing this dataset is a helpful contribution that will facilitate future metric development in this sub-field.
The proposed metric, SEED, demonstrates significantly stronger correlation (Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson) with human judgments compared to existing metrics.
The proposed Pairwise Hinge Loss ($L_{\text{pair}}$) is conceptually straightforward and demonstrates consistent quantitative and qualitative improvements across multiple reconstructed architectures.
weaknesses: Ad-hoc metric integration: SEED is computed as a simple average of three highly disparate metrics: Object F1, Cap-Sim, and EffNet. Because these metrics have different scales, bounds, and underlying distributions (e.g., EffNet correlation can range from -1 to 1, while Object F1 is bounded between 0 and 1), simply taking their arithmetic mean lacks mathematical rigor and theoretical justification.

High computational overhead and reproducibility risk: To evaluate a model with SEED, one must run several heavy, off-the-shelf neural networks, including MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer, and EffNet. This introduces massive computational overhead for evaluation. Furthermore, the metric is highly dependent on specific weights and model versions, making it prone to performance drift and hard to standardize as a benchmark over time.

No analysis of inter-rater agreement: The paper lacks standard statistical metrics (such as Fleiss' Kappa or Krippendorff's Alpha) to evaluate the consensus and reliability of the 22 MTurk annotators. Without this, it is hard to assess the quality of the crowd-sourced human judgments.

Ethical and quality concerns regarding crowdsourcing: Payment of $0.03 per image pair is extremely low. This raises ethical issues regarding fair wages for online annotators and casts doubt on the quality of the annotations, as underpaid workers often rush through tasks, leading to noisier labels.

Evaluation of the loss function on downgraded baselines: In Section C.1, the authors state they had to downgrade the baseline MindEye2 model (reducing the shared latent space dimension from 4096 to 1024 and removing the low-level pipeline) due to hardware constraints. Consequently, the quantitative improvements shown in Table 3 are on a weakened baseline. It remains unclear if the Pairwise Hinge Loss provides any significant benefit to the fully-scaled, state-of-the-art models.

Weak conceptual connection: The paper feels split into two separate ideas: a multi-modal evaluation metric (SEED) and a training loss ($L_{\text{pair}}$) in CLIP embedding space. The link between why a pairwise hinge loss in CLIP space specifically aligns with or optimizes a metric that combines grounding, captioning, and EffNet is not sufficiently explored.

strengths: The paper addresses a critical and timely issue in visual brain decoding: the misalignment of standard evaluation metrics (e.g., 2-way identification, SSIM) with human perception, especially as diffusion-based models achieve seemingly near-perfect scores on existing metrics.

The proposed metric SEED is motivated by neuroscientific findings (two-stage visual attention process) and combines object-level presence (Object F1), high-level descriptive captioning (Cap-Sim), and structural features (EffNet) to create a comprehensive evaluation.

The collection and planned release of a large-scale human evaluation dataset (1,000 image pairs evaluated by 22 annotators on NSD and 50 pairs on GOD) is a strong contribution that will benefit the community.

Detailed analysis of worst-case judgments and systematic failure modes (such as 'semantic near-misses' and 'missing semantic details') provides valuable and actionable insights for visual brain decoding research.
Excellent robustness checks are performed, demonstrating that the metric is robust to the choice of underlying models (e.g., using alternative grounding and captioning models).
weaknesses: High computational complexity and model dependency: SEED relies on several large, pre-trained models (grounding, captioning, embedding, and classification models). Biases, hallucinations, or out-of-distribution failures in these upstream models can directly propagate to SEED, as shown in the paper's own worst-case analysis (Fig. 10).

The individual components (e.g., caption similarity via Sentence Transformers or F1 score of detected objects) have limited technical novelty on their own, although their combination and application to this domain are novel.

The improvement of SEED over the strongest existing single metric (EffNet) is positive and statistically significant, but relatively moderate (e.g., Pearson correlation improvement from 0.748 to 0.813 on NSD).

The metric is primarily focused on semantic similarity; as brain decoding models mature to generate high-fidelity, photorealistic images, a purely semantic-focused metric may lack the sensitivity to evaluate fine-grained pixel-level or structural fidelity. This is acknowledged by the authors but remains a limitation of the current work.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Significance: High-level visual brain decoding models have advanced significantly, but the community is bottlenecked by outdated, saturated, and human-misaligned evaluation metrics (like two-way identification). This paper addresses a highly critical and timely issue.

Well-designed, Multimodal Metric: SEED is built on neuroscientific principles of the human visual system (two-stage visual perception). Integrating object-level presence (Object F1), overall caption-level semantics (Cap-Sim), and global features (EffNet) provides a holistic and interpretable evaluation framework.

Rigorous Validation with Human Studies: The authors collected substantial crowd-sourced and student evaluation datasets (1,000 pairs on NSD, 50 pairs on GOD) with high inter-rater agreement (ICC of 0.84 and 0.93) to validate the proposed metric. SEED achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human judgments across multiple correlation metrics.

Actionable Insights into Failure Modes: Rather than just presenting a number, the authors leverage SEED to identify and quantify critical limitations in 5 state-of-the-art decoding models, discovering issues like 'semantic near-misses' and 'missing semantic details.' This provides concrete future research directions for the brain decoding community.

Thorough Robustness & Ablation Analyses: The paper evaluates robustness against dataset/model shifts and the choice of underlying vision-language models (e.g., switching grounding/captioning models), demonstrating that the metric's performance is stable.
weaknesses: Error Propagation from Off-the-Shelf Models: The metric inherently relies on the accuracy of upstream vision-language models (e.g., MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT). As shown in Fig. 10, distortions in reconstructed images can lead to failures in object detection/captioning (e.g., mistaking an umbrella for a boat), which in turn degrades the reliability of SEED for highly distorted images.

Heuristic Metric Fusion: The integration of the three components in SEED is a simple arithmetic average. While this ensures simplicity and avoids overfitting, the paper would benefit from a discussion or validation on whether a weighted or non-linear combination learned from the human rating dataset could yield even better alignment.

Limited Exploration of Perceptual/Low-Level Similarity: Since SEED focuses heavily on high-level semantics, it does not explicitly capture fine-grained pixel-level or texture-level perceptual similarities. While the authors note this in the limitations, it remains a constraint as brain decoding models mature to generate near-photorealistic outputs.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and timely problem: the inadequacy of current evaluation metrics (such as 2-way identification accuracy or SSIM) for visual brain decoding, which often fail to capture true semantic alignment.

The authors collected a valuable human evaluation dataset consisting of 1,000 ground-truth/reconstruction pairs with 22 raters, which provides a useful benchmark for evaluating similarity metrics in this domain.

The qualitative and quantitative analysis of failure modes (e.g., 'semantic near-miss' and 'missing semantic details') offers interesting and constructive insights into where current diffusion-based brain decoding models fall short.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: The proposed SEED metric is a straightforward, heuristic combination (simple unweighted average) of three off-the-shelf components: Object F1 (MM-Grounding-DINO), Cap-Sim (GIT + Sentence Transformer), and EffNet. There is little theoretical or methodological innovation in how these metrics are integrated.

Unsubstantiated novelty claim: In Section 4.2, the authors claim that 'caption-based evaluation of image similarity has not been previously proposed.' This is incorrect; using captioning models followed by text similarity or parsing to evaluate image similarity or text-to-image alignment is a well-established practice in computer vision.

Vocabulary constraints of Object F1: Object F1 relies on a fixed, narrow vocabulary of 82 categories (mostly COCO classes). For natural scene datasets like NSD, many images contain key objects outside this vocabulary. When the authors tried to relax this limitation using a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), the performance degraded (Table 3), showing that the metric heavily depends on this specific, restricted vocabulary.

Weak baseline comparison: The meta-evaluation compares SEED primarily against fMRI-specific metrics or very old baselines (e.g., SSIM, AlexNet, Inception). It lacks comparisons with state-of-the-art general perceptual and semantic image similarity metrics used in computer vision, such as LPIPS, DreamSim, or direct image-to-image CLIP similarity.

Scale inconsistency: The paper averages Object F1, Cap-Sim (cosine similarity), and EffNet (Pearson correlation) directly to compute SEED. These metrics have different mathematical bounds and distributions, making a direct unweighted average mathematically loose and arbitrary.
The generalization evaluation on the GOD dataset is extremely limited, relying on only 50 image pairs rated by 10 student volunteers, which is too small to draw robust statistical conclusions.

There is a noticeable editing error in Section 2.1, where the sentence 'Instead of freezing the pre-trained diffusion models, NeuroPictor (Huo et al., 2024) fine-tunes the diffusion model to directly condition...' is repeated verbatim at the transition between page 2 and 3, and again in the middle of page 3.
